A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with matching authors, experiments, algorithms and appendix mathematics despite the changed title and expanded scope. Text extraction and visual inspection, including image-only appendix figures, support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v3 reports original Pythia classification experiments measuring attack success, adversarial-training effectiveness, robustness transfer and offense–defense scaling.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds Qwen2.5, StrongREJECT, BEAST, prefix-attack and perplexity-filter evaluations.

M1.justification: Classifier construction, GCG/RandomToken procedures and the adversarial-training algorithm remain substantially unchanged. A limited procedural addition adapts BEAST to classification victims by sampling candidate tokens from a separate small generative model rather than the victim itself (Section 3; Appendix B).

E1.justification: v4 retains all six classification datasets and adds StrongREJECT, extending evaluation to harmful-prompt generation and refusal. It also introduces full-prefix adversarial inputs beyond v3's suffix and 90%-infix scenarios, substantially extending task and threat-model coverage.

E2.justification: v3 evaluates GCG and RandomToken. v4 adds BEAST as an evaluated attack on Pythia and Qwen2.5, including testing GCG-trained defenses against it (Figures 5 and 10). This substantially broadens the comparison suite beyond the original gradient-based attack and random baseline.

E3.justification: v4 adds Qwen2.5 configurations and GPT-4o-judged generative evaluation restricted to initially refused prompts. Reported early-training evaluations change from 12 to 128 GCG iterations, the highlighted trained-checkpoint budget changes from 0.5% to 0.001% of pretraining compute, and offense–defense analysis targets change from 5% to 2% ASR. These are reported setting changes, not proof that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v4 adds GCG-to-BEAST defense transfer, prefix-attack transfer failures and a 21-example perplexity-filter analysis (Section 5.1; Appendix H). It also documents clean-accuracy retention during adversarial training. Existing stronger-GCG, RandomToken-to-GCG and infix-transfer analyses are retained or expanded rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Median/min–max reporting remains, but Figure 2 changes its classification run-count description from five seeds to at least three; the relocated RandomToken comparison specifies three. v4 adds 95% Wilson intervals for StrongREJECT and discloses that prefix attacks used one seed. The PDFs do not establish a uniform reduction or increase in runs.

E6.justification: v4 adds substantial Qwen2.5, StrongREJECT, BEAST and transfer results. Table 1 and Figure 7 replace v3's blanket claim of greater than 83% clean accuracy with lower Helpful/Harmless results, including 0.609/0.594 for 7.6M Pythia. Appendix H newly reports maximum perplexity increasing in only 2 of 21 attacked examples. Revised offense–defense curves use different ASR targets and are not same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: The logit–power-law derivation matches exactly between v3 Appendix C.2.1 and v4 Appendix C.5.1. Adversarial-pool sampling mathematics, FLOP approximations and the ASR-interpolation algorithm are retained. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: v3 concludes that offense has an advantage or approximate parity depending on the setting and that further defense breakthroughs are needed. v4 emphasizes fixed-size offense advantage but introduces a conditional long-run defender advantage as model size increases. It also elevates the distinction between larger models' sample efficiency and lower compute efficiency into a central contribution.

C2.justification: v4 adds hypotheses involving Qwen distillation, Instruct safety training and simple versus sophisticated defenses to explain observed trends. Prefix failures and perplexity overlap introduce substantive applicability limits. The limitations section replaces v3's absolute-cost forecasting discussion with discussion of alternative defenses, broader generative evaluation and task/context complexity.

D1.justification: v4 documents BEAST sampler models, its 25-token suffix and beam size seven, the GPT-4o judge identifier, perplexity-window settings and assumed Qwen pretraining-token counts. It explicitly describes learning-rate decay while retaining the original dataset filtering and adversarial-training hyperparameters. v3's explicit HuggingFace loading API and 200-example compute-discrepancy note are omitted.

R1.justification: v4 adds citations and brief positioning for BEAST, StrongREJECT, Qwen2.5, inference-time robustness and alternative defenses. It removes the Go comparison and Ziegler adversarial-training discussion and softens its criticism of Yang et al. The overall related-work framework and first-large-scale-empirical-study positioning remain.

P1.justification: The title changes from Effects of Scale on Language Model Robustness to Scaling Trends in Language Model Robustness. The abstract, introduction, results narrative and conclusion are extensively rewritten, and appendices are reorganized into subsections by model family, attack and analysis. This exceeds editing associated solely with added experiments.

P2.justification: Main figures are substantially recomposed into paired Pythia/Qwen2.5 comparisons, Figure 1 moves beside the abstract, and RandomToken results move to the appendix. v4 adds a clean-accuracy table and numerous transfer/perplexity displays, redraws axes and legends, and reformats Appendix A examples into full-width entries. Several earlier plot grids and regression panels are omitted.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens evidence beyond Pythia classifiers through Qwen2.5, StrongREJECT and BEAST evaluations. Explicit clean-accuracy results and prefix/perplexity tests expose important applicability limits that v3 left undocumented. These gains outweigh remaining caption inconsistencies, such as Figure 20's attack label. The suggested eventual defender advantage remains a conditional extrapolation rather than a demonstrated outcome.
